title: Compassion can grow
hook: short compassion trainings changed responses to others' pain in lab studies (Klimecki et al., 2013)

segments.voice: Yesterday: easy beats heroic. Did you set tomorrow's practice up so it was already half done? The chair out, the note on the kettle? Day three hundred thirteen.

Some people are just kind. That's how we talk about it. Kindness is a trait, like height or eye color, and you got whatever you got. Your aunt who remembers every birthday was born that way. Your coworker who never notices anyone was born that way too. It's a comfortable idea, because it lets everyone off the hook. But a group of researchers in Germany wondered whether it was true. Could a few days of practice change how a person responds when they see someone else in pain? They taught people a very old practice, and then they put them in a brain scanner and showed them videos of people suffering. Today: compassion can grow.
screen: `SOME PEOPLE ARE JUST KIND.` → `A TRAIT, LIKE EYE COLOR?` → `THE RESEARCHERS WONDERED.`

segments.voice: First, two things that sound alike. Empathy is feeling with someone: their pain lands in you. Compassion is feeling for someone: warmth toward their pain, and a wish for it to ease. The word compassion comes from Latin, com and pati: to suffer with. But the researchers found the difference matters. In studies by Olga Klimecki, Tania Singer and colleagues, people first trained in empathy alone, resonating with others' distress. After watching the videos, they reported feeling worse, and brain areas linked to pain became more active. Then they trained in compassion, the warm wish. Their brain responses shifted toward areas linked to care, reward and connection, and they reported more positive feeling, even while watching the same suffering. A few days of practice made a measurable difference. Second, what they practiced. It was loving-kindness, the Buddhist practice called metta that we met on our visit to Buddhism: bringing someone to mind and silently wishing them well, first someone easy, then a stranger, then someone difficult. Buddhists call compassion karuna, the wish that others be free from suffering. Third, the caution. These are lab studies with small groups, measuring feelings and brain signals, and other studies found training helped people give a little more in a sharing game, but nobody has shown that a weekend turns anyone into a saint. The honest claim is modest: it's trainable. Fourth, why that matters on a Tuesday. If compassion is a trait, burnout means you've run out. If it's a skill, feeling flooded by other people's pain may mean you're practicing empathy without the warmth. You can add the wish. Compassion can grow, the way a muscle does, slowly, with use.
screen: `EMPATHY FEELS WITH. COMPASSION FEELS FOR.` · `EMPATHY HURT. COMPASSION WARMED.` · `METTA: WISHING SOMEONE WELL.` · `MODEST, BUT TRAINABLE.` · then, large: `COMPASSION CAN GROW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a stranger. Maybe someone you saw today: the person at the checkout, a driver, a face on the train. You don't know their name or their day. Picture them for a moment. Then silently wish them well, in the plainest words you have. May your day get easier. May you be well. If you like, add one more stranger. Notice any warmth, and don't worry if there isn't much. The bell holds the time.
Compassion can grow. Not a fixed trait but a skill: feeling for someone, with a warm wish, can be trained. Today's word.
Your line: compassion can grow. Today, pick one stranger in passing, the barista, a tired parent, someone on the bus, and silently wish them well. One rep. Day three hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In loving-kindness practice, drawn from Buddhism, people bring someone to mind and silently wish them well, moving from a loved one to a stranger to someone difficult; researchers have used short versions in lab studies of compassion.

notes: Klimecki et al. (Max Planck, Leipzig): empathy training increased negative affect and activity in anterior insula/anterior midcingulate; subsequent compassion training increased positive affect and activity in medial orbitofrontal cortex, pregenual ACC and ventral striatum. Confirm the summary and which paper is which (2013 Cerebral Cortex vs 2014 SCAN).
Weng et al. 2013: two weeks of online compassion training increased redistribution in an economic game; the script says 'give a little more in a sharing game'. Confirm.
The trainings drew on metta practice; the script calls it loving-kindness from Buddhism and karuna compassion. Buddhist reviewer may want to confirm the karuna gloss.
